landmark_cases.title: Schneckloth v. Bustamonte
landmark_cases.reason: Sets the core Fourth Amendment consent doctrine—consent is a warrant exception and voluntariness is assessed under the totality of the circumstances; knowledge of the right to refuse is not required.

landmark_cases.title: United States v. Matlock
landmark_cases.reason: Establishes third-party consent based on common authority or joint access/control, central to validating a spouse’s consent to enter/search a shared home.

landmark_cases.title: Florida v. Jimeno
landmark_cases.reason: Defines the scope-of-consent inquiry using objective reasonableness—what a typical reasonable person would have understood from the exchange.

landmark_cases.title: Bumper v. North Carolina
landmark_cases.reason: Clarifies that consent must be freely and voluntarily given and that apparent consent obtained through claims of lawful authority (e.g., asserting a warrant) is invalid; frames coercion analysis.

landmark_cases.title: Scott v. Harris
landmark_cases.reason: Provides the principle that clear video evidence can control the factual narrative on review, allowing courts to reject versions of events contradicted by recordings.
